lessons.title: Assessing needs and resources for irrigation
lessons.html:
Matching the system to the farm

Irrigation turns marginal land into high-value production, but it uses scarce water and expensive energy and capital. Developing a suitable system starts with a careful assessment, not with buying pipes.

Water resource

  • Legal right: under the National Water Act 36 of 1998, irrigation water use must be lawful (existing lawful use, general authorisation, or licence). Check registration and allocation with the Department of Water and Sanitation or the irrigation board or water user association.
  • Quantity and reliability: borehole yield tests, dam capacity, river flow in dry years, canal schedules.
  • Quality: salinity, sodium, iron, suspended solids and microbes affect crops, soils and equipment choice.

Soil

Soil depth, texture, infiltration rate and water-holding capacity determine how much water can be applied at a time and how often. Sandy soils need frequent light applications; clay soils accept water slowly and risk runoff with high application rates. Soil surveys with profile pits are essential.

Crop water requirements

Crop water use depends on the crop, growth stage and climate (evapotranspiration). Peak demand in midsummer determines the system capacity needed. Local data from the ARC, irrigation design software or published crop coefficients help estimate requirements.

Topography, energy and labour

  • Slope and field shape influence system choice and pressure.
  • Pumping costs depend on head (height and friction) and flow; electricity tariffs and load-shedding affect scheduling. Solar pumping may suit some sites.
  • Labour availability and skills: some systems need more management than others.

Bring this together in a design brief before talking to suppliers.

lessons.title: Choosing the irrigation system
lessons.html:
System types and their fit

SystemSuitsAdvantagesLimitations
Flood/furrowFlat land, heavy soils, some orchards and sugarcaneLow energy and capitalLower efficiency, needs levelling, labour
Dragline/quick-coupling sprinklersSmall areas, pastures, vegetablesLow capital, flexibleLabour to move, wind affects uniformity
Permanent sprinklersPastures, some orchardsLow labour, frost protection possibleHigher capital
Centre pivotLarge fields of maize, wheat, lucerne, potatoesLow labour, good uniformity, automationHigh capital, circular area, needs suitable soils for application rate
Micro-sprinklersCitrus, subtropical orchardsGood wetting pattern, efficientFiltration needed
DripVineyards, orchards, vegetables, tunnelsHighest efficiency, fertigation, low pressureGood filtration and maintenance needed, rodent damage

Selection criteria

  1. Crop and spacing.
  2. Soil infiltration and water-holding capacity.
  3. Water quality (drip needs clean water and filtration).
  4. Water availability and efficiency needs.
  5. Capital, operating and energy costs over the system's life.
  6. Labour and management skills.
  7. Topography and field shape.

Design principles

Use a qualified irrigation designer, ideally one who works to recognised industry design norms. Key design outputs include system capacity matching peak demand, pipe sizes limiting friction loss, pump selection at its efficient operating point, emitter spacing and pressure for uniform application, filtration, and pressure regulation on slopes. Ask for the design to state expected uniformity and energy use per hectare.

lessons.title: Installation, scheduling and maintenance
lessons.html:
Making the system perform

Installation and commissioning

Check that installation matches the design: pipe sizes, depths, valves, filters, air valves and pressure regulators. Flush lines before attaching emitters. Commission the system by measuring pressures and flows at the pump and at the ends of laterals, and test uniformity with catch cans (sprinklers) or emitter flow measurements (drip).

Irrigation scheduling

Scheduling decides when and how much to irrigate.

  • Soil-based: tensiometers, capacitance probes or neutron probes show soil moisture at root depth.
  • Weather-based: evapotranspiration from a weather station with crop factors.
  • Plant-based: observations or sensors of plant stress.

Aim to refill the root zone before the crop is stressed, without draining water below the roots. Consider rainfall and adjust after rain.

Maintenance

  • Clean and backflush filters; flush laterals regularly.
  • Check and replace worn nozzles and blocked emitters.
  • Treat water where needed to prevent clogging by iron, algae or scale (acid or chlorine injection by trained staff with PPE).
  • Service pumps and motors; check pressure gauges.
  • Repair leaks promptly.

Performance evaluation

Measure water applied (flow meters), yields and energy use. Calculate water productivity (kg per m³) and cost per mm applied. Repeat uniformity tests every season or two.

Safety

Pump stations carry electrical hazards: only qualified electricians work on electrical installations, keep panels closed and dry, and lock out before maintenance. Keep clear of moving pivot towers and drive shafts.

Key points

  • Confirm lawful water use under the National Water Act first.
  • Base design on soil, crop, water quality, topography and costs.
  • Use a qualified designer and commission against the design.
  • Schedule with soil moisture or weather data.
  • Maintain filters and emitters, measure performance and work safely around electricity.
